name: Runner's Knee (Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome)
secondary_queries: pain in front of knee when squatting
seo_title: Runner's Knee Treatment in North Palm Beach | First Rehab
seo_desc: Runner's knee (patellofemoral pain) treatment in North Palm Beach with guideline-based hip and knee strengthening. One-on-one care. Call 561-624-4263.
lede: Runner's knee is an ache around or behind the kneecap that flares with stairs, squats and running, and targeted hip and knee exercise is its best-supported treatment.
what_it_is: Your kneecap, or patella, glides in a groove at the end of your thighbone as you bend and straighten your leg. Patellofemoral pain is an ache around or behind the kneecap that worsens when that joint is loaded in a bent position. The APTA's clinical practice guideline describes it as pain that usually begins without a specific injury and builds with squatting, stairs, prolonged sitting, jumping or running.

Despite the nickname, you do not have to be a runner to get it. Mayo Clinic notes that it mainly affects adolescents and young adults and that females are twice as likely to develop it. Running and jumping sports, sudden increases in training, weakness around the hip and knee, and previous knee surgery all raise the odds. It can affect one knee or both.
symptoms: Dull, aching pain around or behind the kneecap
Pain going up or down stairs
Pain with squatting, kneeling, running or jumping
An ache after sitting for a long time with the knees bent
A popping or crackling feeling in the knee
Pain that comes on gradually, often without a specific injury
causes: Overuse from running and jumping sports
Sudden increases in how long, how often or how hard you train
Weak hip and thigh muscles that affect how the kneecap tracks
Previous knee surgery, especially ACL reconstruction using the patellar tendon
Being female, an adolescent or a young adult

how_therapy_helps.intro: The APTA's 2019 clinical practice guideline for patellofemoral pain recommends exercise therapy that combines hip and knee strengthening to reduce pain and improve function in the short, medium and long term. It supports combining exercise with options such as taping, kneecap mobilization or stretching, and it recommends against knee braces, sleeves and straps and against passive treatments like ultrasound and electrical stimulation. The exercise you do is the core of the plan.
methods: Exercises for the muscles at the back and side of the hip. The APTA guideline notes hip-targeted exercise has shown benefit in the short and medium term, which can help when loading the knee is still painful.
Quadriceps work such as resisted squats or knee extensions, progressed as the joint behind the kneecap tolerates more load.
Tape applied to the kneecap may be added to exercise for short-term pain relief, according to the APTA guideline, to make training more comfortable.
For runners, cues to adjust step rate, foot strike or hip motion, which the guideline lists as an option for easing load on the kneecap.
If your feet roll in more than usual, the guideline supports prefabricated shoe inserts combined with exercise for short-term pain relief, up to about six weeks.
A plan for how much running, jumping and stair work to do while symptoms settle, so you stay active with fewer flare-ups.

first_visit: Your therapist asks when the pain started, what aggravates it and whether your training recently changed. Squatting and stair stepping are key checks, since the APTA guideline uses pain during these movements to identify patellofemoral pain. We measure hip and thigh strength, check quadriceps, hamstring and calf flexibility, look at how the kneecap moves, and watch your control on one leg. Runners may be asked about or shown their stride.
recovery: Patellofemoral pain often responds to a consistent exercise program, but it can be stubborn. The APTA guideline notes that symptoms can recur and persist for years, and that a longer history of pain, higher pain levels and poorer function at the start are linked with slower recovery. The same guideline reports that combined hip and knee exercise reduces pain and improves function over the long term. Keeping up your home exercises after formal therapy ends is one of the most practical ways to limit recurrences.
self_care: Scale back the activities that bring on the ache, such as hills, deep squats and stairs, rather than stopping all exercise
Try lower-impact options like stationary cycling or swimming, as the AAOS suggests
Ice the front of the knee for about 20 minutes after activity if it helps
Stand up and move regularly instead of sitting for long stretches with your knees sharply bent
Increase running distance or intensity gradually once you return
see_a_doctor: Knee pain that is not improving after a few days of rest, or a knee that is getting harder to move (Mayo Clinic)
The knee locks, gives way or clicks painfully (NHS)
Pain that began with a specific fall or twisting injury
Fever with redness, warmth or swelling around the knee
Pain that keeps you from bearing weight

faqs.q: What is the fastest way to heal runner's knee?
faqs.a: There is no shortcut, but the approach with the strongest evidence is a combined hip and knee strengthening program. The APTA's 2019 clinical practice guideline recommends it to reduce pain and improve function in the short, medium and long term. Pairing exercise with smart load management, and short-term aids like taping when they help, tends to work better than rest or passive treatments alone.

faqs.q: Can I keep running with runner's knee?
faqs.a: Many people can keep running in some form while they rehab, as long as distance, pace and terrain are adjusted so pain stays mild and settles by the next day. Hills and stairs are often the first things to reduce. The APTA guideline also lists gait retraining, such as increasing step rate or changing foot strike, as an option for runners with patellofemoral pain.

faqs.q: Does a knee brace help runner's knee?
faqs.a: The evidence does not support it. The APTA's 2019 clinical practice guideline recommends that clinicians not prescribe patellofemoral braces, sleeves or straps for patellofemoral pain. Patellar taping is different: the same guideline says taping combined with exercise may reduce pain in the short term. Strengthening the hip and thigh muscles remains the main treatment.

faqs.q: Why does my knee hurt going down stairs?
faqs.a: Going down stairs loads the joint between your kneecap and thighbone while the knee is bent and your thigh muscles work to control the descent. The APTA's clinical practice guideline lists stair climbing and descent, along with squatting, among the activities that typically reproduce patellofemoral pain. Building hip and quadriceps strength usually makes stairs easier over time.

faqs.q: Is runner's knee the same as IT band syndrome?
faqs.a: No. Runner's knee, or patellofemoral pain, is felt around or behind the kneecap at the front of the knee. IT band syndrome causes pain on the outside of the knee where the iliotibial band crosses the thighbone. Both are common in runners and both respond to hip strengthening, but the exam and exercise emphasis differ, so an evaluation helps sort out which one you have.

faqs.q: How long does runner's knee last?
faqs.a: It varies widely. Some people improve within weeks of starting a structured exercise program, while others have symptoms for much longer. The APTA's 2019 guideline notes that 50% to 56% of adolescents still report knee pain two years after diagnosis, and that people with longer-standing or more severe pain tend to recover more slowly. Starting targeted exercise sooner may help.

signOrSymptom: pain around or behind the kneecap

notes_for_reviewer: ICD-10 M22.2 (Patellofemoral disorders) verified on icd10data.com; billable children M22.2X1/M22.2X2/M22.2X9. The approximate synonyms list 'patellofemoral syndrome' but not the exact phrase 'patellofemoral pain syndrome'; confirm this matches clinic coding.

The 2019 JOSPT CPG recommendations (grades A to C) were read from the jospt.org full text via a scraper; please spot-check the taping (B), orthoses (B), bracing (B, against), biophysical agents (B, against) and gait retraining (C) statements.
Patellar taping is listed as a method; confirm clinicians are comfortable offering it, since the brief restricts modalities.
AAOS also calls PFPS 'jumper's knee', which conflicts with the patellar tendinitis page; that alias was deliberately left out.
Mayo's 'females twice as likely' is the only prevalence-type figure in the body.
Cleveland Clinic page on runner's knee could not be fetched (rate limited), so it is not cited.
